title: Ron And Tammy

jokes.text: Old Gus's retirement speech concludes: 'And I've come to the conclusion that I've completely wasted mine.'
jokes.setup: A retirement ceremony is underway with warm, sentimental speeches about brightening lives and hearts — standard feel-good farewell fare.
jokes.punchline: Old Gus reflects on his life and concludes he's completely wasted it.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant cold-open subversion. The ceremony sets up every sentimental beat we expect, then Gus punctures it with devastating honesty. The economy is excellent — it lands in one short sentence after a long wind-up. The bleakness is unexpected and specific enough to feel genuinely funny rather than cheap nihilism.

dialogue.speaker: Old Gus
dialogue.line: You know, I've been thinking about my time here, and I want to say something from the heart.

dialogue.speaker: Old Gus
dialogue.line: This job, this town, these people... they've meant everything to me.

dialogue.speaker: Old Gus
dialogue.line: But I gotta be honest with you all. I've wasted my whole life.

dialogue.speaker: Old Gus
dialogue.line: I should've traveled. I should've learned to dance. I should've told my ex-wife I was sorry.

dialogue.speaker: Old Gus
dialogue.line: Instead, I just sat around complaining about everything.

jokes.text: Old Gus: 'And just for the record, I never ever liked being called old Gus. I didn't understand it when I was in my 20s and I sure hate it now.'
jokes.setup: Having just said he wasted his life, Gus pivots to a seemingly smaller grievance — his nickname.
jokes.punchline: He's harbored resentment about this nickname his entire adult life and is only saying so now.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of grievances works beautifully — from existential (wasted life) to petty (hated nickname). The detail that he didn't understand it in his 20s adds a lovely absurd dimension. Strong character-specific specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Old Gus
dialogue.line: They've called me 'Old Gus' for fifty years.

dialogue.speaker: Old Gus
dialogue.line: I've always hated it, even when I was young.

jokes.text: Old Gus: 'So go to hell, every single one of you. Screw Pawnee and screw your damn shoes.'
jokes.setup: The retirement speech has now fully abandoned any pretense of sentimentality.
jokes.punchline: Gus signs off by telling the entire assembled crowd and the city to go to hell, and specifically cursing their shoes.
jokes.explanation: The tricolon of 'go to hell / screw Pawnee / screw your shoes' is pitch-perfect escalation. The specificity of 'screw your damn shoes' — tying it back to his job as a shoeshine man — is what elevates this from a generic angry-old-man bit into something memorably specific and structurally elegant. Strong quotability and rewatch value as a cold open.

dialogue.speaker: Old Gus
dialogue.line: I've been shining shoes in this town for forty-seven years. It's been an honor to serve you all.

dialogue.speaker: Old Gus
dialogue.line: But you know what? Nobody appreciates it. Nobody says thank you. You just walk in, drop your shoes like I'm some kind of servant.

dialogue.speaker: Old Gus
dialogue.line: My wife left me. My kids won't call. And for what? For what?!

dialogue.speaker: Old Gus
dialogue.line: These shoes! These cursed shoes! I've wasted my entire life on these shoes! To hell with these shoes! To hell with all of you!

jokes.text: Leslie's talking-head reaction: 'Old Gus is classic.'
jokes.setup: We've just witnessed a retirement ceremony devolve into bitter cursing from an old man.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's cheerful, oblivious summary: 'Old Gus is classic.' Her optimism is completely tone-deaf to what happened.
jokes.explanation: Three words doing heavy lifting. Pure character comedy — only Leslie Knope would describe a man who just cursed an entire room as 'classic.' The character integration score is near-perfect because this joke only works with Leslie's specific brand of relentless positivity.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, that was... spirited!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I think he called us all 'incompetent weasels.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But in a fun way!

jokes.text: April is texting during the subcommittee meeting; when confronted, she says 'You.' She's texting Leslie, who is sitting right there.
jokes.setup: Leslie scolds April for texting during the meeting.
jokes.punchline: April reveals she's texting Leslie — who is sitting directly across from her — as an act of passive-aggressive disengagement.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly distilled April Ludgate behavior. The joke is entirely in the character — her sullen refusal to engage with the meeting even on the terms of normal human communication. Extremely economical. The secondary beat of 'She's texting me' from Leslie (bewildered but not angry) adds a layer.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, are you texting during the meeting?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Then who are you texting?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy's sitting right there!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's faster than talking to her.

jokes.text: Tom runs the subcommittee meeting by asking: 'Would you rather be able to fly or speak fluent French?'
jokes.setup: Leslie puts Tom in charge of 'keeping the momentum going' on the planning subcommittee.
jokes.punchline: Tom's idea of productive momentum is a game of Would You Rather.
jokes.explanation: Solid character joke. Tom's complete inability to take work seriously is well-established, and the specific choice of 'Would You Rather' question feels authentic to him. Donna's immediate enthusiastic 'French' is a nice button.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I was texting. I'm bored.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking-head about the library: 'Pawnee's Library Department is the most diabolical, ruthless bunch of bureaucrats I've ever seen. They're like a biker gang. But instead of shotguns and crystal meth, they use political savvy. And shushing.'
jokes.setup: Leslie describes the library department with escalating danger rhetoric — 'diabolical,' 'ruthless,' 'biker gang,' 'shotguns and crystal meth.'
jokes.punchline: The terrifying arsenal turns out to be 'political savvy' and 'shushing.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup is a masterclass in misdirection — it builds genuine menace through escalating criminal imagery, then deflates it with two perfectly mundane library-specific things. 'And shushing' as the final beat, delivered as a standalone sentence, is excellent structural economy. Highly quotable and a signature Parks and Rec bit. Justifies the 8+ score by matching the reference anchor for sharp, unexpected, and highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, I'm leaving you in charge. Keep this meeting productive.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You got it, Leslie. I'm on it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay everyone, would you rather fight one horse-sized duck or a hundred duck-sized horses?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Tom, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Keeping things productive. Now answer the question.

jokes.text: Leslie announces 'I don't want to cause a panic' and then immediately announces: 'News flash, we're screwed. We got a big problem with the library. Punk ass book jockeys.'
jokes.setup: Leslie says she doesn't want to cause a panic.
jokes.punchline: She immediately causes a panic in the most alarmist language possible, including 'punk ass book jockeys.'
jokes.explanation: The ironic self-contradiction lands well, and 'punk ass book jockeys' is genuinely funny phrase-coinage. The specificity of Leslie's simultaneous desire to appear calm and inability to hide her distress is perfect character work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The library? They filed for the library? No, no, no. Not the library. Anyone but the library. We could lose the rec center, the animal shelter, the old folks home—I mean, those would be tragedies, obviously—but the library? The library is sacred. The library is where knowledge lives. Where dreams are born. Where I lost my virginity!

jokes.text: After Leslie describes the library as the worst group ever assembled — mean, conniving, rude — she adds: 'and well read, which makes them very dangerous.'
jokes.setup: A list of terrible qualities: mean, conniving, rude.
jokes.punchline: Being well-read is presented as equally if not more threatening than the moral failings.
jokes.explanation: A clean extension of the library joke. Works as both a character beat (Leslie's worldview is so local-government-centric that being well-read reads as an instrument of power) and a standalone structural joke. The 'which makes them very dangerous' tag is a perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The library is a scary place. Librarians are like bikers, except instead of leather jackets and motorcycles, their weapons are the power of shushing.

jokes.text: An unnamed character's talking-head: 'I actually think a library would be nice that close to my house. But I'm not about to say that in there.'
jokes.setup: Everyone in the room is performing outrage about the library's bid for lot 48.
jokes.punchline: One person privately admits they think a library would actually be fine — but social pressure forces them to keep it to themselves.
jokes.explanation: Good mockumentary structural joke — the talking head undercuts the in-room groupthink. Slightly weakened by not being attributed to a specific named character, reducing the character integration score. The premise is solid but familiar.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Punk ass book jockeys.

jokes.text: Ben/Chris reaction: 'That's terrific. Or is that awful? He hates her, but he knows her. Everything's okay. Or is it just the same? You're thinking out loud again. Am I? I am.'
jokes.setup: Leslie learns that the library's new deputy director is Ron's ex-wife.
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately spirals into an out-loud internal monologue she doesn't realize she's saying aloud.
jokes.explanation: Lovely Leslie character comedy. The rapid oscillation between optimism and doubt, delivered as an accidental monologue, is very specific to how she processes information. The self-realization moment ('Am I? I am.') is a good button.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Librarians are the worst. They're always shushing people, they smell like old books, and they have an unhealthy relationship with due dates.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But the most dangerous quality a librarian can have? Being 'well read.' Because then they actually know things, and they'll correct you in front of everyone.

jokes.text: Ron's talking-head: 'Of course, that bitch of an ex-wife is working for the library now. That is perfect. The worst person in the world working at the worst place in the world.'
jokes.setup: Ron learns his ex-wife Tammy now works for the library, the institution he hates most.
jokes.punchline: He calls it 'perfect' — the worst possible convergence of evils has occurred, stated with dry inevitability.
jokes.explanation: Ron's dry delivery and the escalating symmetry ('worst person / worst place') is satisfying. The word 'perfect' doing ironic work is very Ron Swanson — he names catastrophe with stoic precision.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I mean, obviously libraries are terrible and a complete waste of taxpayer money.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: But... like, hypothetically... if someone wanted to go to a library and just read books in a quiet place for a few hours, that wouldn't be the worst thing in the world.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Does she have any weaknesses?' Ron: 'What do you mean no? Everybody has one.' Ron pause, then: 'Not machines.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if Tammy has any weaknesses, expecting useful intel.
jokes.punchline: Ron first says no, then qualifies: 'Not machines' — implying Tammy is not a machine, but barely.
jokes.explanation: Tight two-beat structure. The pause between 'everybody has one' and 'not machines' does the heavy lifting — Ron has to recalibrate his worldview to accommodate that Tammy may be the exception. The implication that she might qualify as a machine is absurdist but grounded in Ron's sincere belief.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tammy is coming to Pawnee? Tammy Two or Tammy One? Please say Tammy Two. Oh my God, what if it's both Tammys? What if they've formed some kind of Tammy alliance against me? That's insane. That's actually insane. I need to call Tom. I need to call everyone. I need to move to Canada.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, you're spiraling.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm not spiraling, you're spiraling!

jokes.text: Ron's talking-head: 'I honestly believe that she was programmed by someone from the future to come back and destroy all happiness.'
jokes.setup: Ron is asked to explain his feelings about Tammy.
jokes.punchline: He offers a Terminator-style origin story for his ex-wife's evil, delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ron Swanson joke. The Terminator riff is a clever frame, but what elevates it is the specificity of 'to destroy all happiness' — not the world, not democracy, just happiness. This is Ron's personal cosmology rendered in a single sentence. Delivered deadpan, it lands as one of his great talking-head lines. Justifies 8+ because it's character-perfect, highly quotable, and absurdist without being random.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: She works at the library? The library? That's the perfect alignment of my two greatest hatreds.

jokes.text: Ron's talking-head: 'On my death bed, my final wish is to have my ex-wives rushed to my side, so I can use my dying breath to tell them both to go to hell, one last time.'
jokes.setup: Ron is reflecting on his two ex-wives both named Tammy.
jokes.punchline: His dying wish is not reconciliation or peace — it's to deliver one final 'go to hell' to both of them.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The subversion of the deathbed-wish trope is perfect — the romantic trope (ex-wife called to bedside) is hijacked for the exact opposite of closure or love. 'One last time' implies he's said it many times before and wants one more. Extremely quotable, absolutely character-specific. Only Ron Swanson has this relationship with hatred as a life-organizing principle. Scores in the 8-9 range are fully justified.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What are Tammy's weaknesses?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: She's not human. She's a machine. Machines don't have weaknesses.

jokes.text: Ron's talking-head (immediately after the death-bed speech): 'Would I get married again? Absolutely. If you don't believe in love, what's the point of living?'
jokes.setup: Ron has just described wanting to spend his dying breath cursing his ex-wives.
jokes.punchline: He pivots to declaring unambiguous romantic optimism: he'd absolutely get married again, because love is the point of living.
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition with joke 15 is the engine here. Ron sincerely holding both 'I want to tell my ex-wives to go to hell' and 'love is the point of living' without apparent contradiction reveals the comedic depth of his character. The structure is nearly perfect — the pivot is abrupt, which is exactly right. This is the kind of joke that gets better on rewatch because you anticipate the whiplash. Justifies 8+ through structural excellence and character complexity.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tammy isn't human. She was built in a secret government lab in 1987 as the perfect weapon. She has a titanium skeleton, hydraulic muscles, and a heart made of ice. They sent her back in time to destroy my life, and she succeeded. She's a Terminator, but worse—she's a Taminator.

jokes.text: Leslie before meeting Tammy: 'I'm just looking forward to a thoughtful debate with Tammy, about the relative merits of Parks versus Libraries. And in case something bad goes down, I wore my sharpest rings. This one will tear you up.'
jokes.setup: Leslie frames the meeting as a professional policy discussion.
jokes.punchline: She has also dressed for combat, specifically wearing a ring chosen for its ability to lacerate.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Leslie bit. The two-register joke (diplomatic framing + covert war-preparedness) is perfectly structured, and 'This one will tear you up' as a deadpan aside about a ring is a great button. Leslie's optimistic framing colliding with her barely-suppressed survivalist instincts is pure character gold. Justifies 8+ through character integration and structural elegance.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have a fantasy where each of my ex-wives is on her deathbed, and I get to say goodbye. So I show up and say, 'Hey.' And she says, 'Ron, I'm so sorry for everything I did wrong.' And I say, 'I know,' and I leave. That's the fantasy.

jokes.text: Leslie arrives at the library and Tammy immediately confronts her about overdue book fees: '$3, Missy.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has girded herself for battle. She expects Tammy to open with something manipulative or hostile about the lot.
jokes.punchline: Tammy's opening salvo is a $3 overdue fine — genuinely petty library bureaucracy deployed as an opening move.
jokes.explanation: Smart structural joke. After all the build-up about the library being a terrifying biker gang, Tammy's actual opening weapon is a $3 fine. The bathos is earned and perfectly calibrated. Leslie's overreaction ('dirty pool, B.S. move') makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have nothing but contempt for my first two wives. But I have a good feeling about wife number three.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'That's why everybody hates the library. Here's your $3. See you in hell.'
jokes.setup: Tammy has presented a trivial $3 fine. Leslie has treated it as a declaration of war.
jokes.punchline: Leslie pays, delivers a dramatic 'See you in hell,' and storms off — over a library fine.
jokes.explanation: A callback to Leslie's earlier war-preparedness ('See you in hell' echoes 'this one will tear you up') and a great character beat. The disproportionate drama of 'see you in hell' over $3 is perfectly Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going into the library. I may not come out alive. But if I don't, tell my story. Tell them I died doing what I loved.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Also, I brought weapons. Jewelry weapons. Pointy earrings, a sharp brooch. If things get ugly, I'm going in swinging.

jokes.text: Tammy: 'We government gals have to watch each other's backs, right?' Leslie's talking-head: 'I know this is a trap but I don't know how.'
jokes.setup: Tammy clears Leslie's fines and offers camaraderie.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's private confession that she is certain it's a trap but cannot identify the mechanism. Her instincts are good but she has no actionable intelligence.
jokes.explanation: Very strong economy — eight words that perfectly capture Leslie's position. Funny because it's also the correct read of the situation. The precision of 'but I don't know how' is what makes it quotable and memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Library employee
dialogue.line: You owe $3 in overdue fees.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Three dollars? That's it? I thought I was being arrested for murder!

dialogue.speaker: Library employee
dialogue.line: No, just the fees.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh thank God. I was worried for nothing.

jokes.text: Tammy: 'Ron tends to exaggerate when it comes to me. I swear, I don't have cloven feet.'
jokes.setup: Tammy is trying to appear reasonable and normal to Leslie.
jokes.punchline: She volunteers the very specific denial 'I don't have cloven feet' — which raises the question of why that denial is necessary.
jokes.explanation: Classic 'too specific denial' comedy. By mentioning cloven feet unprompted, Tammy implies Ron may have claimed she has them, and also that it's a plausible enough accusation to warrant addressing. Excellent character establishment for Tammy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A three dollar fee? THREE DOLLARS? Do you know what this means?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It means you owe the library three dollars?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It means war, Ben. It means war.

jokes.text: Andy's shoeshine pitch: 'Shine, shine, shine your shoes? What do you say, sir? Ma'am, shoeshine? I won't look up your skirt.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just started his new job as shoeshine guy.
jokes.punchline: He pitches potential customers and casually includes 'I won't look up your skirt' as a selling point — implying this is a concern people have and a distinction worth noting.
jokes.explanation: Very Andy Dwyer. He's trying hard but lacks any filter between thought and word. Treating 'I won't look up your skirt' as a standard sales feature implies his brain went through a list of customer concerns and chose to address the worst one first. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: You can't just joke about that! This is a library! These are books!

dialogue.speaker: Library employee
dialogue.line: I was just messing with you. I'm actually totally fine with it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Oh. Well... that's... I may have overreacted.

jokes.text: Andy to Ann: 'Just trying the rat race. Chasing the cheese. Racing the rats. To get the cheese.'
jokes.setup: Ann asks how things are going. Andy tries to use a business idiom.
jokes.punchline: He mangles 'rat race' into an increasingly confused elaboration that circles back to cheese twice.
jokes.explanation: Andy's broken idiom is a reliable comedy engine. The specific failure mode here — he restates the metaphor, gets confused, inverts it, then redundantly reaffirms his goal — is beautifully observed incompetence. 'Enough business talk' as the pivot away is a good button.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: Leslie, I think you're doing a great job.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? Why would you say that? What do you want? Are you dying? Did you poison me?

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: I'm just trying to be nice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, stop it. It's creepy and it's making me very uncomfortable.

jokes.text: Andy's excuse for slow business: 'It is definitely due to... the economy.' Mark: 'I've been hearing a lot of people say that a lot, about a lot of stuff.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to seem credible about why his shoeshine stand has no customers.
jokes.punchline: Andy deploys 'the economy' as a catch-all explanation; Mark's deadpan response acknowledges the universal 2009 cliché.
jokes.explanation: A well-timed observational joke about the 2009 habit of blaming the economy for everything. Mark's triple-'a lot' response is a nice deadpan button. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: I do not have devil hooves. These are normal feet.

jokes.text: Andy offers Mark a discount 'because you're a friend of Ann's.' Mark: 'I'm more than a friend of Ann's.' Andy: 'Not for long.'
jokes.setup: Mark asserts that he's more than just Ann's friend — he's her boyfriend.
jokes.punchline: Andy casually predicts Mark won't hold that position for long. It's a sincere threat delivered without menace, which makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: Tight three-word punchline. Andy's complete lack of awareness about social norms (threatening a man's relationship while shining his shoes) is very funny. The economy is excellent — 'Not for long' does exactly the right amount of work.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna be a professional shoeshine person. I promise I won't look up your skirt.

jokes.text: Andy's talking-head about his old audition tapes to Survivor and Deal or No Deal, followed by the actual tape: 'Hi, my name is Andy Dwyer, and I would be a perfect contestant for Deal or No Deal.'
jokes.setup: Ann describes Andy's pre-employment history as sending reality TV audition tapes.
jokes.punchline: We see (implied by context) the actual tape, where Andy delivers a completely generic, unpersuasive audition pitch.
jokes.explanation: The visual of the audition tape (implied) and Andy's earnest, substance-free pitch ('I would be a perfect contestant') is very funny. The joke is in how little effort he put in — he offers no reason, just confidence. Good character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm not running in the rat race, I'm running in the rat... marathon. Which is longer and harder, so I'm winning.

jokes.text: Leslie's planning pitch includes: 'a lovely sitting area for kids with asthma to watch other kids play.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is describing her ideal park — swings, basketball courts, state of the art.
jokes.punchline: She adds a designated area for children with asthma to spectate from the sidelines. The thoughtfulness makes it worse.
jokes.explanation: Dark and surprising. The premise is Leslie is caring and thorough — she thinks of everyone. But the specificity of 'kids with asthma watching other kids play' is unintentionally bleak and sad, which is exactly the joke. Her follow-up about her own 'prolonged mall slut phase' doubles down on the unexpected self-disclosure. Justifies 8+ through originality and the perfect balance of Leslie's oblivious earnestness producing something genuinely uncomfortable.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, the economy is really bad right now. People aren't spending money. It's a tough market out there.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Honestly, I have no idea what I'm talking about. I just hear people say that stuff and I repeat it.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'If I'd had a park like that when I was growing up, I probably wouldn't have gone through such a prolonged mall slut phase.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been describing her ideal park in warm, civic-minded terms.
jokes.punchline: She reveals a surprising personal history as justification — a 'prolonged mall slut phase' she attributes to insufficient park infrastructure.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout lines. 'Prolonged mall slut phase' is a perfectly chosen phrase — the word 'prolonged' does enormous comic work by implying duration and effort, while 'mall slut phase' is unexpected from Leslie Knope. The causal logic (inadequate parks caused this) is absurd but delivered with complete Leslie sincerity. Extremely quotable and highly character-specific. Fully justifies a top-tier score.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Ann and I are together now.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Well, I'm gonna punch you in the face!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Just kidding. You seem like a good guy.

jokes.text: Leslie tells Ron: 'What's it like to stare into the eye of Satan's butt hole?' after she's met Tammy.
jokes.setup: Ron asks Leslie how her meeting with Tammy went, expecting adult professional language.
jokes.punchline: Leslie uses a vivid, scatological metaphor for evil that reveals her real feelings about the encounter.
jokes.explanation: Funny phrase-coinage. 'Satan's butt hole' is deliberately crude in a way that's incongruous with Leslie's usual professional presentation. The 'eye of' construction (borrowing from 'eye of the storm') elevates it slightly. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: His job was applying to reality TV shows.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Look at Mark and me. We slept together, talked about it. We're friends.' Ron: 'You slept with Brendanawicz?'
jokes.setup: Leslie uses her friendship with her ex-hookup Mark as evidence that Ron and Tammy could achieve closure.
jokes.punchline: Ron's reaction is complete incredulity that Leslie slept with Mark — he had no idea. The subplot revelation lands as a punchline.
jokes.explanation: Strong reaction beat. The joke is in how casually Leslie drops this information while trying to make a different point. Ron's 'You slept with Brendanawicz?' is the perfect stunned response to an overshare. Works within the season's ongoing subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Andy Dwyer, and I'm here to audition for Wheel of Fortune. I've been preparing for this my whole life. I'm incredibly lucky. One time I found a twenty dollar bill in my jacket pocket. I didn't even know it was there. That's luck. I'm basically a luck machine.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I've also been studying the wheel. I know all the letters. A, B, C, D, E... I could go on, but I don't want to show all my cards before the audition. I'm also very good at guessing. My guess right now is that this audition is going great.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Tammy and I don't work. We are oil and water. Or oil and TNT and C-4 and a detonator and a butane torch.'
jokes.setup: Ron uses the cliché 'oil and water' to describe his incompatibility with Tammy.
jokes.punchline: He immediately finds that insufficient and escalates the metaphor through increasingly explosive materials.
jokes.explanation: Beautiful escalation structure. The joke starts with a cliché and then systematically destroys it by replacing it with a chain of genuinely explosive things. The list — TNT, C-4, detonator, butane torch — each one adding to the absurdity while also being technically coherent (these things are all explosive or incendiary). Ron's expertise in such things is consistent with his character. Justifies 8+ through structural excellence and escalation craft.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: My ideal park would have a special area for kids who can't participate in normal activities. We'd call it the 'Participation Trophy Garden.'

jokes.text: Ron's head snaps up mid-conversation: 'She's here, isn't she?' — followed by a long pause before Tammy enters.
jokes.setup: Ron has been insisting he wants nothing to do with Tammy and that nothing good can come of them meeting.
jokes.punchline: He senses her presence before she appears — animal instinct born from years of bad experiences. The pause sells the dread.
jokes.explanation: Purely visual/structural comedy. The beat of Ron going still and quietly asking 'She's here, isn't she?' plays like a horror movie moment and is funny for that reason. The long pause before she enters amplifies it. Strong character integration — this is exactly how Ron Swanson's trauma would manifest.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I was a mall slut in the '90s.

jokes.text: After Ron and Tammy have a prolonged, apparently extraordinary moment of eye contact, Leslie says: 'Good. Good start.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has arranged this meeting and is watching Ron and Tammy's reunion unfold.
jokes.punchline: Her oblivious optimistic commentary — 'Good. Good start' — on what is clearly a dangerous, volatile reconnection reveals she has completely misread the situation.
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie reaction. Three words of inappropriate cheerleading. Works because the audience can see what she cannot — that this 'good start' is anything but.

jokes.text: Donna's talking-head: 'You were not here when they got divorced. I was. Those two are crazy. And you opened the gates. To crazy town.'
jokes.setup: Leslie congratulates herself for getting Ron and Tammy to speak.
jokes.punchline: Donna has witnessed the divorce and delivers a bleak warning: Leslie has 'opened the gates to crazy town.'
jokes.explanation: 'Crazy town' as a destination is a well-worn phrase, but the structural pause — 'You opened the gates. To crazy town.' — is good delivery. Donna's authority here (she witnessed the divorce) gives the warning weight.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You slept with Mark Brendanawicz?!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Mark Brendanawicz! That's like sleeping with a piece of cardboard that got sad!

jokes.text: Leslie's confessional: 'Frankly, I think Ron was acting like a baby. A little bit. What is he afraid of? Tammy's just a woman. A nice woman. You know, she's not a murderer. She's not a dragon.'
jokes.setup: Ron has been having a visible meltdown over Tammy's presence.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's defense of Tammy — 'She's not a murderer. She's not a dragon.' — are the lowest possible bars for 'nice woman,' while the specificity of 'dragon' is funny.
jokes.explanation: 'She's not a dragon' is a rewatch bonus — once you see how the episode ends, the bar Leslie sets here is hilariously low. The escalation of her rationalizations ('not a murderer... not a dragon') mimics someone trying to convince themselves of something they don't fully believe.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tammy and I are like oil and water.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: We don't mix. We repel each other.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: If you put us in a container together, the container will explode.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: The explosion will be so powerful it will take out a city block.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: And then birds will flee in terror.

jokes.text: Leslie defends Tammy: 'She's not a murderer. She's not a dragon.' Then: 'It's really good to see you, Ron.' Tammy: 'You've aged horribly.' Ron: 'You... son of a bitch.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been defending Tammy as a normal, non-murderous, non-dragon woman.
jokes.punchline: Tammy opens with 'You've aged horribly,' and Ron's response is not anger but something closer to recognition and affection — 'You... son of a bitch.' — as if this is foreplay.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully constructed. Leslie's defense is immediately followed by Tammy's first words proving her wrong in the most specific way. But the real joke is Ron's response — 'You... son of a bitch' isn't angry, it's almost tender. He recognizes her, and that recognition is tinged with something complicated. Excellent character work that pays off everything established about these two. Justifies 8+ through structural elegance, character specificity, and the complexity of the emotional beat.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Leslie, you cannot reunite Ron and Tammy. That is crazy town.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What do you mean? It'll be fine.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: No. Crazy town. Population: you.

jokes.text: Donna's talking-head immediately after Ron and Tammy's combustion: 'Who set the bed on fire?'
jokes.setup: The implication is that Ron and Tammy's reunion has been violent and/or sexual.
jokes.punchline: Donna's rhetorical question about a burning bed implies a level of chaos that goes well beyond what we've seen — and suggests this has happened before.
jokes.explanation: Six words doing a lot of work. 'Who set the bed on fire?' as a matter-of-fact question suggests this is a known recurring phenomenon and Donna just wants to assign responsibility. The specificity of 'the bed' (not 'a bed') implies familiarity with this disaster scenario. Very high economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tammy. You look exactly the same.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: So do you. Except fatter.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's woodworking dust, not fat.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: Sure it is.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'When you meddle in someone's personal life, it's just so... rewarding.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has clearly caused a disaster by facilitating Ron and Tammy's reunion.
jokes.punchline: Her talking-head refuses to admit failure, instead framing the disaster as 'rewarding.'
jokes.explanation: The sarcasm is ambiguous — Leslie may actually mean it. Her inability to recognize her mistakes is a core character trait, so the line walks a funny line between genuine obliviousness and ironic self-awareness.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Why is the bed on fire?

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: Because you touch yourself at night.

jokes.text: Ron's morning talking-head: 'Good morning, Jerry. That is a beautiful sweater vest.' — delivered with completely unusual warmth, signaling that something has changed in Ron.
jokes.setup: Ron normally has nothing positive to say to Jerry. The audience expects his baseline dismissiveness.
jokes.punchline: He's inexplicably chipper, complimenting Jerry's sweater vest. The joke is in the wrongness of it.
jokes.explanation: Effective character comedy through contrast. Ron's usual persona makes 'That is a beautiful sweater vest' to Jerry a alarming signal. The joke requires knowledge of Ron's character but pays off well for regular viewers.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, Ron and Tammy Two got back together, which is great for them, terrible for literally everyone else, but I'm choosing to see the silver lining here, which is that at least they'll be destroying each other's lives instead of ours.

jokes.text: Ron bribes a young person with $20: 'You look like you could use $20.' Kid: 'Why?' Ron: ''Cause you're a kid and kids always need money. I need money.' Ron: 'That's why you're my favorite.'
jokes.setup: Ron is in an unusually good mood and trying to spread it.
jokes.punchline: His logic for giving out money — 'you're a kid, kids need money, I need money, that's why you're my favorite' — is circular and nonsensical, delivered with complete confidence.
jokes.explanation: Solid absurdist moment. Post-sex Ron trying to be generous but having no real framework for generosity creates funny illogic. Not as sharp as other Ron jokes in this episode.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: April, I'm in an excellent mood. Here's twenty dollars.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why are you giving me money?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Because you're a child, and children like money for candy and... whatever it is you people do.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm not a child, Ron. I'm a grown woman.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Well, you're certainly not acting like one.

jokes.text: Ron's talking-head: 'When Tiger Woods feels invincible, he wears a red shirt and black pants. Ron wears the same thing after he had sex. I'm a simple man. I like pretty dark-haired women and breakfast food. But this stock photo I bought at a framing store isn't real. Today I got the real thing. A naked Tammy made me breakfast this morning.'
jokes.setup: Ron explains why he's wearing red and black — a Tiger Woods parallel implying a peak performance state.
jokes.punchline: He reveals the photo of a happy breakfast on his wall is fake/stock, but today the real version happened — Tammy made him breakfast. The escalation from Tiger Woods metaphor to 'a naked Tammy made me breakfast' is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ron moment. The stock photo of breakfast food bought at a framing store is an unexpected and very specific detail — Ron has idealized a domestic scene with a prop. 'A naked Tammy made me breakfast this morning' lands hard because it's both extremely TMI and exactly the thing Ron would consider peak living. 'I'm a simple man. I like pretty dark-haired women and breakfast food' is a highly quotable distillation of Ron's values.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Tiger Woods wears red on Sundays because it's his power color. It gives him confidence.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have the same ritual, but for a different reason. I wear red on Sundays so people know to stay away from me.

jokes.text: Ron's talking head: 'I'm a simple man. I like pretty dark-haired women and breakfast food. But this stock photo, I bought at a framing store, isn't real. Today I got the real thing. A naked Tammy made me breakfast this morning.'
jokes.setup: Ron appears unusually content; he begins describing his simple pleasures (dark-haired women, breakfast food) and gestures to a framed stock photo.
jokes.punchline: The stock photo admission is funny on its own; the revelation that today he got the real thing — 'a naked Tammy made me breakfast' — confirms he slept with his dangerous ex-wife and is blissfully unaware of the consequences.
jokes.explanation: This is a multi-layered gem. Ron having a framed stock photo of a woman and breakfast food is already absurdly funny. The pivot to 'today I got the real thing' and the matter-of-fact 'a naked Tammy made me breakfast' is perfectly timed revelation comedy. Character integration is at its peak — only Ron Swanson. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I like breakfast food. I like hash browns, I like wheat toast, I like bacon. Why do I have to choose? I want all the breakfast foods.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That family photo on my desk? Stock photography. I have no children and I've never been to the Grand Canyon.

jokes.text: Andy to Mark: 'Break up with her and tell her to go out with me.' Mark: 'Can I ask you another question? Why did I come to you for advice?'
jokes.setup: Mark has come to Andy for relationship advice about Ann.
jokes.punchline: Andy's advice is to break up with Ann so Andy can date her himself. Mark immediately regrets asking.
jokes.explanation: Clean Andy joke. He has no filter between his desires and his 'advice.' The structure is tight — Andy's answer is so bad that it immediately raises the question of why anyone asked. Mark's self-recrimination is a good button.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I woke up this morning and Tammy was making breakfast naked. I should have photographed it.

jokes.text: Andy's talking-head: 'I've never taken the high road. But I tell other people to. 'Cause then there's more room for me on the low road.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just given Mark surprisingly sensible advice to take the high road.
jokes.punchline: In his talking-head, he reveals he has never taken the high road himself and directs others to it purely for self-interested reasons.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines, and possibly the most quotable. The logic is airtight and the self-awareness is unexpected from Andy. 'There's more room for me on the low road' is clever, memorable, and works as a standalone quote. The structure is nearly perfect — the reversal of 'take the high road' as altruistic advice into a self-serving strategy is elegant comedy writing. Justifies 8+ easily.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Tom, I need some relationship advice. April's been distant lately.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, here's what you do. You buy her something expensive. Very expensive. Like, from my store.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's not relationship advice, that's a sales pitch.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, Andy, I'm just saying — if you want to fix things with April, you gotta show her you care. And the best way to do that is to give me money. I mean, give her a gift. From Rent-A-Swag.

jokes.text: Ron to Leslie: 'I can't thank you enough for sticking your nose where it didn't belong.' Leslie: 'I knew it.' Ron: 'We made love.'
jokes.setup: Ron approaches Leslie with what sounds like a sarcastic complaint about her meddling.
jokes.punchline: He actually means it genuinely — Tammy and Ron slept together — and cuts straight to 'We made love' without transition.
jokes.explanation: Good structural misdirection. The sarcastic-sounding opening leads Leslie (and the audience) to expect a complaint, then flips to sincere gratitude with the punchline reveal. Ron using the phrase 'made love' is also funny — it's slightly too formal and romantic for his usual register.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You gotta take the high road, Andy. Let other people bring you down to their level.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, that makes sense.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That way, the low road is completely clear for me.

jokes.text: Ron describes sex with Tammy: 'It was so intense. I didn't know where my flesh stopped and hers began. Our marriage was always a complete disaster, but we did have that, the two of us. It's like doing peyote and sneezing slowly for six hours.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to politely receive Ron's good news without details.
jokes.punchline: Ron provides details anyway, culminating in the metaphor: sex with Tammy is like 'doing peyote and sneezing slowly for six hours.'
jokes.explanation: The standout line of the episode. 'Doing peyote and sneezing slowly for six hours' is extraordinary comedy writing. It uses three incongruous elements (a hallucinogen, a mundane bodily function, and a very specific duration) to describe an indescribable sensation. It's original, unexpected, completely Ron Swanson (he would reach for a frontier-adjacent metaphor), and deeply quotable. The specificity of 'slowly' and 'six hours' is what makes it sing rather than just being random. Fully earns a near-9 craft score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're welcome, Ron. I'm glad I could help.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Thank you, Leslie. Thank you for your meddling. It means so much to me that you can't respect boundaries or let people handle their own problems. I really appreciate you inserting yourself into my personal affairs without being asked.

jokes.text: Ron, mid-overshare: 'She knows her way around a penis.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been trying to gracefully exit the conversation about Ron and Tammy's sex life.
jokes.punchline: Ron adds a final clinical endorsement before Leslie can escape.
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — six words. The matter-of-fact delivery and the very specific but entirely clinical phrasing ('knows her way around') makes it funnier than a cruder version would be. Works partly because of context (Leslie desperately trying to change the subject).

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't like to brag, but I'm excellent in bed. I'm a heavy sleeper.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I truly believe that everyone should be friends with their exes. I can't even tell you how many of my exes' weddings I've been to.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is cheerfully advocating for exes remaining friends.
jokes.punchline: The evidence for her position is that she has attended many of her exes' weddings — to other people. The implication is a string of relationships that went nowhere for her.
jokes.explanation: Quietly sad and funny. The gap between Leslie's optimistic framing and what the detail actually reveals (she's been to many exes' weddings because they all married someone else) is the joke. Subtle but effective character work.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's like doing heroin, except instead of a needle in your arm, it's a Tammy in your soul.

jokes.text: Donna reacts to Ron and Tammy reading divorce papers: 'Three fistfuls of hair? That's not even possible.' Leslie: 'Well, I'm too classy to say I told you so, Donna. So I wrote it on a post-it.'
jokes.setup: Donna reacts to a violent-sounding detail in Ron and Tammy's divorce papers. Leslie has been waiting to gloat.
jokes.punchline: Leslie claims class prevents her from saying 'I told you so' — but she wrote it on a post-it note, which she has presumably produced.
jokes.explanation: Two jokes layered here. Donna's 'three fistfuls of hair — that's not even possible' (dark comedic detail from the divorce papers) is followed by Leslie's post-it gloat. The post-it joke is particularly good — it's both very Leslie (organizational, prepared, finds loopholes in her own stated values) and structurally clever. The subversion of 'I'm too classy to say I told you so' by immediately doing exactly that is a clean joke. Justifies 8+ through character integration and the post-it being a perfect Leslie prop.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I know what I'm talking about. I've been around the block.

jokes.text: Tammy to Ron: 'I mean you spend so much time worrying about this park. But really, who cares? At the end of the day what does it matter if the lot becomes a park or a museum or a mega church?' Ron: 'Or a library.' Tammy: 'Nobody said library.'
jokes.setup: Tammy lists various possible uses for the lot, conspicuously omitting library while trying to downplay the stakes.
jokes.punchline: Ron supplies 'library' to complete the obvious list, and Tammy's response 'Nobody said library' is a textbook guilty deflection.
jokes.explanation: Tight structural joke. 'Nobody said library' when it's obviously what everyone is thinking is a perfect comic beat. The innocent deflection reads as comically guilty. Good economy and strong character moment — Tammy's manipulation through omission, exposed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I think it's great to be friends with your exes. I mean, why wouldn't you want to maintain those relationships?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've been to like, what, five of my exes' weddings? Six?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I caught the bouquet at two of them.

jokes.text: Ron is caught. When pressed: 'We have discussed a trade.' Leslie: 'For what?' Ron: 'Excuse me.' Beat. 'More sex.'
jokes.setup: Leslie confronts Ron about whether he's giving Tammy the lot. He admits to discussing a 'trade.'
jokes.punchline: After a dignified pause, he admits the trade consideration is 'more sex.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best structured exchanges. The pause ('Excuse me') creates perfect comedic timing — Ron needs a moment to compose himself before admitting this. 'More sex' as a two-word answer to 'for what?' is devastatingly economical. The whole exchange demonstrates Ron's simultaneous dignity and complete loss of self-control around Tammy. Justifies 8+ through structure, economy, and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: These divorce papers say Tammy tried to kill me by wrapping me in a carpet and rolling me off a cliff.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Ron, that's... how is that even physically possible?

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: That's what the judge said.

jokes.text: Tammy to Leslie: 'Les, there are two kinds of women in this world. There are women who work hard and stress out about doing the right thing and then there are women who are cool.'
jokes.setup: Tammy is explaining her worldview and implicitly positioning Leslie as uncool.
jokes.punchline: Her two categories — women who do the right thing vs. 'cool' women — is a villain's manifesto that exposes her values completely.
jokes.explanation: Effective character establishment for Tammy. The binary she creates (right vs. cool) is a clever inversion of conventional wisdom — she's basically saying virtue is for losers.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm not the type of person who says 'I told you so.' I'm way too classy for that.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: But I do write it down. So I have a record of it.

jokes.text: Tammy: 'You could either be a Cleopatra or you could be an Eleanor Roosevelt.' Leslie: 'What kind of lunatic would wanna be Cleopatra over Eleanor Roosevelt?'
jokes.setup: Tammy frames her two female archetypes as Cleopatra (glamorous, powerful through seduction) vs. Eleanor Roosevelt (principled, earnest).
jokes.punchline: Leslie's reaction — genuine bafflement that anyone would choose Cleopatra — is a perfect character statement. From Tammy's perspective it's an obvious choice; from Leslie's it's insane.
jokes.explanation: The joke lives entirely in Leslie's response. The fact that she doesn't even consider Cleopatra a viable option — genuine lunacy in her view — is perfect Leslie Knope characterization. She identifies completely with the earnest doer, not the glamorous schemer.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: We could put in a big parking lot, or a small parking lot, or a medium parking lot.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What about a library?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I never said that.

jokes.text: Ron defends libraries: 'Some people like libraries.' Leslie: 'I can't even believe it. Some people like libraries.' Ron: (same words, two completely different registers)
jokes.setup: Ron is now defending the institution he has described as the worst place in the world, because Tammy has gotten inside his head.
jokes.punchline: The words 'some people like libraries' from Ron is the funniest possible thing he could say. Leslie's echo of the same words expresses her horror.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional callback comedy. Everything established earlier about Ron's hatred of libraries makes 'some people like libraries' from him feel like hearing a priest blaspheme. The repetition by Leslie — the same four words expressing completely different emotions (his capitulation, her horror) — is brilliant structural comedy. This is exactly what a 8+ callback moment looks like. Justifies the score through structural mastery and perfect character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Scotch.

jokes.text: Ron's talking-head: 'I'm so screwed now. Her hooks are in my brain.' Beat. 'She has all the power and I have nothing. I'm so little.'
jokes.setup: Ron has been broken by Tammy's influence and must acknowledge it.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm so little' as the final statement of a man who has been established as the most self-sufficient, stoic person in Pawnee.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely great comedic moment. 'I'm so little' from Ron Swanson — a man whose entire persona is built on bigness, stoicism, and self-sufficiency — lands as one of the most unexpected and funny admissions in the episode. The escalating vulnerability of 'she has all the power and I have nothing' building to the devastating 'I'm so little' is a perfect comedic escalation. Character integration is nearly perfect. Justifies 8+ clearly.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: There are three kinds of women: the hot ones, the smart ones, and the ones who are neither. Leslie is the third kind.

jokes.text: Ron: 'I don't think I can [break up with her]. We would just end up naked. And I'd give her your lot and my house and God knows what else. I have no control over my actions.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks why Ron can't simply break up with Tammy.
jokes.punchline: Ron outlines the doom scenario: any contact leads to nudity, then to property transfer, then to unknown catastrophe.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation. The sequence of consequences — nudity, property transfer, 'God knows what else' — establishes the complete logic of the Tammy doom spiral. Ron's admission of having 'no control over my actions' is both funny and character-perfect for a man who prizes self-reliance above all.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: You can be either a seductive role model or a virtuous role model.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Those are my only two options? Seductive or virtuous? Why can't I be both? Why can't I be neither? Why does it have to be so binary?

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: Choose.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Virtuous! Virtuous, obviously virtuous!

jokes.text: Leslie's impression of herself: 'It took years of intense, focused hatred to get over her. And now I've undone all that great work.'
jokes.setup: Ron is lamenting Leslie's facilitation of his reunion with Tammy.
jokes.punchline: 'Years of intense, focused hatred' as a therapeutic framework — and 'great work' for that hatred — frames his recovery as labor undone.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ron Swanson joke. The idea that 'intense, focused hatred' is a form of therapeutic self-work — and that this hard work has been ruined — is both absurd and completely true to his character. 'Great work' for the hatred is the key word choice. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: The key to manipulation is patience and understanding human weakness. You identify what someone wants, then you control the supply.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: It's basic psychology. Works every time.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: That's... that's horrifying.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: It's standard library procedure. The late fees, the hold times, the 'lost' reservation requests. We invented the game.

jokes.text: Leslie parrots back Ron's earlier advice to her: 'It's just coffee, Ron. She's changed, Ron. I let Mark nail me and we're still friends.' Ron: 'I never... I would never use those words.' Leslie: 'Point taken.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is taking responsibility for enabling the situation by repeating her own (now embarrassing) earlier advice.
jokes.punchline: She uses language Ron would never use ('nail me'), and he objects specifically to the word choice rather than the content. 'Point taken' as a concession while they both agree she bears responsibility.
jokes.explanation: Good callback with a nice twist. The funniest element is Ron objecting to word choice rather than the substance — he can process the reality but not Leslie's vocabulary for it. 'Point taken' as a shared acknowledgment of her culpability without further argument is a good button.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: You should join the library. You'd make an excellent librarian.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Absolutely not. I would never work at the library. Never.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: But you love reading and organizing things.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I don't care if it's the perfect job. I'm not working at the library. The Parks Department is where I belong.

jokes.text: Leslie awkwardly paraphrases herself to Ron: '"It's just coffee, Ron." "She's changed, Ron." "I let Mark nail me and we're still friends."' Ron: 'I never... I would never use those words.' Leslie: 'Point taken.'
jokes.setup: Ron accurately quotes Leslie's advice back to her in a devastatingly direct paraphrase.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's quoted version includes 'I let Mark nail me' — which Ron objects to as not his wording; Leslie immediately concedes the point rather than the substance.
jokes.explanation: Strong callback comedy. Ron's objection being purely about word choice ('I would never use those words') rather than the substance — he agrees she slept with Mark, just not the phrasing — is very Ron. 'Point taken' from Leslie conceding his grammar rather than her culpability is good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: Leslie, I've enjoyed our time together as government gals, but I'm ending this alliance effective immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? Why? We were just bonding over bureaucratic procedures!

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: Precisely. It was getting too friendly. I have a reputation to maintain.

jokes.text: Andy to Mark: 'So how's the shoeshine game?' Mark: 'I'm on a break.' Andy: 'One of the many advantages of owning your own business.' Mark: 'You know that's not your situation, right?'
jokes.setup: Andy has started a shoeshine station and refers to it as 'owning his own business.'
jokes.punchline: Mark gently corrects this delusion. Andy seems to have misunderstood the nature of his employment situation.
jokes.explanation: Consistent Andy joke. His aspirational self-image (entrepreneur) clashing with reality (he has a stool in a government building) is funny but familiar territory for this character.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I may have been too harsh on the library. It turns out they have a very nice reading room, and the librarian has excellent posture.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, are you... attracted to the librarian?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm simply acknowledging that the library has redeeming qualities I previously overlooked.

jokes.text: Andy asks Donna who she'd choose between Mark and himself. Donna: 'I'm not sure. Why don't you spin around for me.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks Donna to adjudicate his romantic competition with Mark for Ann.
jokes.punchline: Donna turns it into an audition, asking him to spin — as if this is a legitimate evaluation criterion.
jokes.explanation: Good Donna moment. Her complete willingness to participate in Andy's nonsense on her own terms is consistent with her character — she'll engage, but she'll do it her way.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you're defending libraries?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have nothing against libraries. Librarians, on the other hand, are the bane of my existence. They promote the accumulation and retention of books and reading. I'm against that.

jokes.text: Tammy: 'What Ron wants to do is leave here right now. Go to the sleaziest motel in town and wrap himself around me like a coiled snake.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just said Ron is 'completely over' Tammy.
jokes.punchline: Tammy contradicts this with an extremely specific and vivid prediction of what Ron actually wants, including 'like a coiled snake.'
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'the sleaziest motel in town' and 'like a coiled snake' elevates a simple counter-claim into something vivid. Tammy's confidence in her own prediction is the engine — she knows exactly what Ron wants better than he does.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: She has all the power. I am but a tiny, helpless man.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'See? He's completely over you.' Ron barely manages to look away from Tammy. Tammy: 'I'm pretty sure he does.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to defend Ron's disinterest while Ron is visibly failing to be disinterested.
jokes.punchline: The gap between Leslie's claim and Ron's visible behavior (the audience can infer he is transfixed) is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Primarily a visual/physical comedy beat inferred from context. Leslie's delusional advocacy for someone who is visibly failing to support her case is a good dramatic irony joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I can't break up with Tammy. She has this power over me. In a sexual haze, I'd give away everything - my land, my guns, my woodworking tools. Everything I've worked for my entire life.

jokes.text: Mark to Ann: 'I understand that this Ann situation is awkward. But I like you a lot as a dude.' Then: 'I'm still in love with Ann. I couldn't have been more upfront about that.'
jokes.setup: Mark is attempting to take the high road and be civil with Andy.
jokes.punchline: He tries to be gracious and then immediately undermines it by declaring he's still in love with Ann and was 'upfront' about it — as if this is somehow the mature position.
jokes.explanation: Decent character moment for Mark — his idea of 'taking the high road' still includes professing love for Andy's girlfriend. Not as sharp as the stronger jokes in this episode.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I feel powerless.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron Swanson, you are the most powerful man I know.

jokes.text: Mark to Andy: 'I think you're a cool dude too. I like you as well. But I'm still in love with Ann. I couldn't have been more upfront about that.'
jokes.setup: Andy tells Mark he likes him as a person and hopes they can be mature and be friends.
jokes.punchline: Mark immediately responds with 'but I'm still in love with Ann' as if this is completely compatible with friendship — and claims he couldn't be more upfront.
jokes.explanation: Mark's complete inability to read the room — presenting love for your rival's girlfriend as a neutral fact in a friendship offer — is a good character beat. 'I couldn't have been more upfront' is a nice self-justifying irony.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you're the strongest man I know. You can do anything.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, I appreciate that. But there is one thing I cannot do. I cannot say no to Tammy. She is my kryptonite.

jokes.text: Andy to Mark after Leslie intervenes in Ron/Tammy situation: 'Is punching allowed on the high road?'
jokes.setup: Andy had been told to take the high road in his rivalry with Mark.
jokes.punchline: He asks if violence is permissible within the high road framework — a sincere question, not rhetorical.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Andy question. He's trying to follow the rules he was given but needs clarification on edge cases. The sincerity of 'Is punching allowed on the high road?' implies he's been thinking about this carefully and has a specific use in mind. Excellent economy and character integration. Good callback to the earlier high road bit.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You said we need to 'get our shit together.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I did not say that!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Your exact words.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I would never say that in a professional setting!

jokes.text: Tammy: 'Baby, don't you see what's happening here? She's manipulating you because she's jealous of me and the things I get to do to your body and face.'
jokes.setup: Tammy is accusing Leslie of manipulation.
jokes.punchline: Her evidence: Leslie is jealous of 'the things I get to do to your body and face' — a phrase that is both sexual and implies something almost violent. 'And face' is the unexpected addition.
jokes.explanation: 'And face' is the key comedic word here. 'Body' is expected; 'and face' suggests something beyond conventional romance, consistent with the earlier implication of their physically chaotic relationship.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm not at my shoeshine stand because I'm at a business conference. I'm expanding into the boot market.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You don't own a shoeshine stand.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Not with that attitude, I don't.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'You want Ron. That's what this is all about.' Tammy: 'No, that's insane.' [pause] 'Fine, I had one dream, but no, no.'
jokes.setup: Leslie accuses Tammy of wanting Ron back, not just the lot.
jokes.punchline: Tammy's flat denial collapses almost immediately into a partial confession ('Fine, I had one dream') before rallying.
jokes.explanation: The near-instantaneous crumbling of Tammy's denial is well-structured comedy. 'Fine, I had one dream' as a partial concession immediately walked back is a good cringe beat. The speed of the collapse is funnier than a slow reveal would be.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Andy, you don't own a business. You work for me.

jokes.text: Ron to Leslie after she puts his needs first: 'No woman has ever done that for me before.' Leslie: 'I'm sure that's not true.' Ron: 'You see the kind of women that I choose.'
jokes.setup: Ron is moved that Leslie prioritized his wellbeing over the lot.
jokes.punchline: Leslie tries to reassure him; his response — 'You see the kind of women that I choose' — is a complete self-own that doubles as an explanation of his entire romantic history.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character moment. Ron's response is simultaneously self-aware and completely in denial — he acknowledges his terrible pattern but frames it as an explanation rather than a problem to solve. 'You see the kind of women that I choose' is both an apology to Leslie and a complete Ron Swanson worldview in seven words. Justifies 8+ through character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay Donna, I need you to be the judge. Who's more attractive, me or Mark?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Spin around.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Both of you, spin around. I need to see all angles.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Okay, you can stop. I've made my decision.

jokes.text: Ron: 'If I'm not down in 5 minutes, it's only because I'm receiving a pleasure so intense...' (trails off as he returns to Tammy)
jokes.setup: Leslie has successfully gotten Ron to end things; Ron tells her to wait downstairs.
jokes.punchline: He leaves the door open (literally and figuratively) with 'if I'm not down in 5 minutes' — establishing that his resolve may not last 300 seconds — and the trailing 'so intense...' implies he already knows he will fail.
jokes.explanation: Good structural joke. The 5-minute hedge is self-aware failure planning. The trailing sentence signaling he already knows the outcome is funny because Ron normally never admits weakness.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: You know what? You're right. I am too good for Ron. I deserve better than this pathetic man who works in government and makes no money.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: I'm leaving him.

jokes.text: Andy has put up a sign: 'Andy and Ann's Family Shoeshine.'
jokes.setup: Andy has been trying to win Ann back by becoming a responsible business owner.
jokes.punchline: He's already incorporated Ann into the business name without her knowledge or consent, assuming the relationship outcome he wants.
jokes.explanation: Solid visual gag. The sign reveals Andy's magical thinking — he's planned the partnership before getting agreement. The word 'Family' is the detail that pushes it further (he's not just assuming a business partnership, but a family).

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: You're telling me Leslie Knope volunteered to do this?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No. Leslie volunteered to do it. I'm making her do it.

jokes.text: Ann confronts Andy about the photos: 'You might wanna take these pictures down.' Andy: 'What? It's fine. What did I...' Ann: 'All of it!' Andy: 'I'm gonna.' Ann: 'Now!' Then: 'Give me the bikini one.' Andy: 'The teeny one?' Ann: 'Bikini one.'
jokes.setup: Andy has apparently hung up multiple photos of Ann (and possibly himself with Ann) at his shoeshine station.
jokes.punchline: The negotiation over which photo to take down first and Ann's specific instruction 'the bikini one' (and Andy's clarifying 'the teeny one?') escalates the absurdity of the situation.
jokes.explanation: The cringe escalation of the photo situation is effective. The 'teeny one?' clarification implies there are multiple bikini photos and Andy needs to identify which specific one she means. The absurdity compounds well.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: Ron doesn't want a woman. Ron wants a snake. A big, long snake that he can keep in a cage and feed dead things to.

jokes.text: Leslie and Ron leave the library at speed. Leslie notices: 'Is part of your mustache missing?' Ron: 'Yes.' Leslie: 'Walk.' Ron: 'There's a push pin in your face.' Leslie: 'Leave it in. Can't you walk faster?' Ron: 'My legs are shorter than yours.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Leslie are making a quick exit from the disastrous Tammy confrontation.
jokes.punchline: The accumulation of injuries — missing mustache, push pin in face — reveals the meeting was physically catastrophic. The exchange of observations ('leave it in') delivered while speed-walking is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Excellent physical comedy sequence delivered entirely through dialogue. Three details: (1) missing mustache, (2) push pin in face, (3) Leslie's leg-length remark. Each escalates the absurdity. 'Leave it in' as Leslie's response to a push pin in her face is a great character-specific joke — she's too focused on escape to care about the wound. The leg-length complaint from Ron is a final humanizing absurdity. Justifies 8+ through structure and escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So you're saying I should take the high road?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's what I'm saying.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But is violence permitted on the moral high ground?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, Andy. No violence.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What about light violence?

jokes.text: Ron's quiet talking-head: 'We had a good run.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just escaped from the Tammy catastrophe — missing part of his mustache, push pin incident implied.
jokes.punchline: 'We had a good run' — a phrase typically used for something that lasted a long time and ended naturally, applied to his mustache (or his sense of dignity).
jokes.explanation: Four words, perfect economy, extremely Ron Swanson. 'We had a good run' applied to his mustache (his most iconic physical feature) treats his facial hair as a companion or colleague who has served honorably. The stoic acceptance of an absurd loss is pitch-perfect character comedy. One of the cleanest jokes in the episode. Justifies 8+ through near-perfect economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: You want Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I do not want Ron!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I mean, not in real life. But I did have this dream once where we were on a sailboat and he made me laugh so hard I fell overboard and he dove in after me and—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to stop talking now.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'You didn't kill Tammy, did you?' Ron: 'I'm afraid she can't be killed.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if Ron managed to end things with Tammy.
jokes.punchline: Ron's phrasing — 'I'm afraid she can't be killed' — treats 'killing' as a literal possibility that was simply beyond his means, rather than a figure of speech.
jokes.explanation: Great callback to the Terminator framing of Tammy. 'She can't be killed' delivered with genuine regret implies Ron attempted it (or at least considered it) and found her indestructible. The callback to the earlier joke about her being a future-programmed machine is implicit and satisfying. Justifies 8+ through economy, dark humor, and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, wait downstairs.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Why? What's going on?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm about to experience something so pleasurable, so intense, so extraordinarily satisfying...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, what are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm going to sand this desk.

jokes.text: Leslie and Ron toast: 'To exes... may they always stay that way.' Then Ron's roast of Tammy: 'She's a great... bitch.' 'Every time she laughs, an angel dies.' 'Even telemarketers avoid her.' 'Her birth was payback for the sins of men.'
jokes.setup: Leslie invites Ron to properly vent about Tammy.
jokes.punchline: Ron's escalating anti-Tammy epithets build from mild ('great bitch') to cosmic ('her birth was payback for the sins of men').
jokes.explanation: Strong escalation sequence. Each epithet tops the last: 'even telemarketers avoid her' is a great specific detail (telemarketers call everyone). 'Her birth was payback for the sins of men' is the peak — a grand theological statement about one woman's existence. The escalation structure is well-crafted and the individual lines are highly quotable. Justifies 8+ through originality of individual lines and structural escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm going to call it Treat Yo Self Enterprises.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, no. April and I broke up. I should probably change that.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: How about... Andy and April's Awesome Company?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, that's still weird. Okay, just Andy's Awesome Company.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? I'm keeping it. Andy and April's Awesome Company. That way she has to think about me every time she sees a business card.

jokes.text: After all the cosmic epithets, Ron's final word on Tammy: 'But you know, the worst thing about her... she works for the library.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just delivered an escalating series of cosmic insults about Tammy's fundamental evil.
jokes.punchline: The single worst thing about her, topping all of these, is her professional affiliation: the library.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke and a near-perfect closer. The entire Ron-and-Tammy mythology, plus the entire library-as-enemy mythology, plus Ron's temporary defection to library sympathy, all converge in a single sentence. Having just described Tammy as an angel-killer, a cosmically born agent of evil and a telemarketer-repelling force of darkness — the WORST thing about her is her job. This simultaneously (1) restores Ron's full hatred of the library, (2) reveals how deeply the library-hatred runs (worse than being an actual force of evil), and (3) closes the episode's thematic circle. The structure is impeccable: the buildup of cosmic insults makes the mundane punchline devastating. Fully justifies the top craft score in this episode.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron! What happened to you?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't want to talk about it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Your mustache is gone!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I said I don't want to talk about it.

tmdb_overview: Leslie is upset when she learns the library department wants to take over her lot. Making matters worse, the library is run by Ron's ex-wife Tammy, who still has a powerful emotional hold on him. Meanwhile, Andy gets a job in hopes of winning Ann back.
insight: Ron's terror of his ex-wife sustains 81 jokes across 22 minutes without mercy.
